title: Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing
gist: At GOTO Copenhagen, Xin Yao argued technical debt is the price of learning by doing rather than poor engineering, and that agentic AI coding now produces software faster than teams can build shared understanding, turning debt repayment into a sociotechnical 'learning debt' problem.

themes.theme: Debt as learning, not bad code

insights.claim: Xin Yao argues technical debt arises from designing software with incomplete knowledge and is the price of learning by doing; it becomes problematic only when software fails to catch up with new learning.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Reframes debt metrics: the risk is unrepaid learning, not debt per se.
insights.quote: yesterday’s good understanding becomes today’s debt
insights.locator: Debt isn’t about poorly written code

insights.claim: Shipping knowingly imperfect code can be a deliberate business strategy because it generates business feedback, user feedback and revenue sooner.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Speed-to-market with planned repayment is rational; judge teams on repayment discipline.

insights.claim: The relevant question about technical debt is not whether to incur it but whether the learning it enables justifies its cost and whether it is actually repaid.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Useful diligence lens for evaluating engineering organizations.
insights.locator: Debt can be a good communication

insights.claim: Drawing on Kent Beck's 'Earn and Learn', Yao argues every feature removes future optionality, and teams that keep producing features, including with LLMs, eventually spend all capacity paying interest on code and can no longer ship features.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: AI-accelerated feature output may hit a maintenance wall that erodes long-run velocity.
insights.locator: Yao referred to Kent Beck’s article

insights.claim: Delaying design commitments to the last responsible moment preserves options; per Kent Beck, waiting is holding an asset, not laziness.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Optionality value in architecture parallels real options in finance.
insights.quote: waiting is not laziness; waiting is holding an asset

insights.claim: Xin Yao argues agentic coding lets software production outpace human understanding, making code a 'fossil record' of agents' decisions while humans remain accountable for consequences.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Accountability gaps from AI-written code create latent operational and liability risk.
insights.quote: Code increasingly becomes a fossil record of agents’ decisions, while humans remain accountable for its consequences.

insights.claim: Local productivity gains from AI coding can create collective costs — more code, weaker ownership and growing gaps in shared understanding — described in a study of developer discourse as 'a tragedy of the commons'.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Headline AI productivity numbers may mask organization-level costs.

insights.claim: With agentic coding, repaying technical debt requires closing the gap between what software actually does and what teams understand it to do, making it a sociotechnical rather than purely technical task.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Demand shifts toward tools for code comprehension, ownership and knowledge-sharing.

insights.claim: Small batches and tight feedback loops help teams retain memory of initial design decisions and continuously repay old debt with new learning.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Delivery practices remain a mitigant for AI-era debt accumulation.
